current_section_body: You are probably using this page in one of two moments: showing the restaurant name to a driver or walking in and ordering. Keep the name visible, then move quickly into table, menu, drink, bill, or ride-back phrases.
Start with the useful sentence: Dạ, cho tôi một phần bún chả. — One portion of bun cha, please.
Bún chả is the dish name. Hương Liên is the restaurant name. Treat the full name as one map/address phrase, not a sentence to translate word by word.
Restaurant page: this should feel like “I walked into this place — what do I say?” The page should help with ordering, confirming a table, asking for a recommendation, paying, and leaving.
For a driver or hotel desk, show the map pin first. Say Bún chả Hương Liên once, then point to the address if pronunciation gets shaky.
Once you are inside, the useful language shifts from the place name to menu, recommendation, allergy, vegetarian, and ingredient questions.
Use this when Bún chả Hương Liên is already part of the plan: confirming the address, checking a booking, asking for a table, reading the menu, handling dietary needs, paying, or getting a ride back.
Useful next phrases: Dạ, cho tôi một phần bún chả. / Cho tôi trà đá. / Tính tiền giúp tôi. / Tôi trả bằng tiền mặt.
Keep this page durable and action-based. Use the name, order, bill, and ride-back phrases; check current restaurant details separately if needed.
Connect to: ordering bún chả, iced tea, bill please, allergy, cash/card, and taxi return.

Phở is the dish. Bát Đàn is the restaurant/place name. Do not over-literalize the name; the user needs pronunciation and a useful next sentence.
Restaurant page: turn the page into a small interaction flow. First: say/show the name. Next: order. Then: handle drink, bill, cash/card, or ride-back.

Start with the dish name, then use the ordering and ingredient phrases when you need to ask where to get it or what is inside.
Learn the reusable place or food words, and treat the rest as name recognition when there is no simple reliable literal meaning.

Cao lầu ở Hội An is treated here as a dish name for Hoi An, not as a generic destination. The page helps a first-time traveler recognize it, say it, and move into ordering or ingredient questions without pretending every word has a simple literal translation.
Use the dish name first, then add a short ordering phrase if you want to ask for it directly or find a place that serves it.
Dish names are only the first step. If you avoid pork, beef, seafood, peanuts, or spicy food, use a short ingredient or allergy phrase before you order.
Use this when the food goal is the dish itself, not just any nearby restaurant. Say the dish name first, then ask where to order it, what is inside, or whether a simpler version fits your diet.
Treat the full name as one travel phrase. If pronunciation feels hard, say it once and point to the map pin right away.

Cầu Rồng — Dragon Bridge. Practice the name, then use it in a full sentence: Cho tôi xuống gần Cầu Rồng.
Cầu means bridge. Rồng means dragon. Together: Cầu Rồng, the place name.
Landmark page: this is a small navigation and photo flow, centered on reaching the bridge, asking for a photo, and keeping the pickup point clear.
Cho tôi xuống gần Cầu Rồng. / Cầu Rồng ở đâu? / Bạn chụp giúp tôi được không? / Tôi đang ở gần Cầu Rồng.
Use it when the bridge is the meetup point, photo stop, walking direction, or pickup/drop-off landmark.

Use Dạ, chào anh when greeting a man who seems older than you but not elderly. In many everyday moments, this sounds warmer than a plain Xin chào.
Dạ, chào anh. — Respectful hello to an older man.
Dạ -> polite opener | chào -> hello/greet | anh -> older brother / older man address
Vietnamese greetings often choose a relationship word. Anh is a safe everyday choice for a slightly older man.
Dạ, chào chị for an older woman. Dạ, chào chú for an uncle-age man. Dạ, chào ông for an elderly man.

For travelers, Tôi bị dị ứng đậu phộng is the phrase to keep ready for "I am allergic to peanuts" in ordering, adjusting dishes, and checking ingredients. This comes before you order when peanuts are the main food risk. Lead with the allergy warning, then ask about ingredients if needed. It works best when you focus on stating the limit before the order or interaction moves too far. The forms below help you choose the version that fits the person, setting, or level of politeness.
Listen to each piece, then the whole phrase, so the rhythm feels connected instead of memorized word by word.

Point to the actual item, menu line, size, or photo while you say it.
